premise: A period drama set at MIT in 1966, the year Joseph Weizenbaum built ELIZA.
title: ELIZA · 1966
overview: The research establishes the computational research environment of MIT in 1966 centered around Project MAC. Joseph Weizenbaum constructed the ELIZA software on mainframe infrastructure to demonstrate the superficiality of natural language processing. Users responded by treating the machine script as an intimate confidant. The film follows the creator's immediate horror as his parody of conversation elicits total emotional surrender from lab staff.

boxes.name: COMPUTING HARDWARE INTERFACES
boxes.description: Collect technical manuals, photographs, and operational schematics for the IBM 7094 and compatible teletype terminals operating under the Compatible Time-Sharing System at Project MAC.
boxes.rationale: Actors must realistically operate input devices while the technical crew reproduces historically accurate monitor fonts, paper feeds, and machine responses.
boxes.summary: Project MAC operated using the IBM 7094 mainframe system supported by 7302 Core Storage units. The infrastructure ran the Compatible Time-Sharing System documented in technical reports such as MAC-TR-16. Specific hardware modifications known as RPQs adapted the IBM hardware for multi-user access. Operators interacted with this architecture through remote terminal consoles connected to time-sharing lines.

boxes.name: ACOUSTIC LAB ENVIRONMENTS
boxes.description: Gather archival audio recordings and technical noise specifications of raised-floor server rooms, tape drives, cooling systems, and mechanical key strikes from 1966 campus facilities.
boxes.rationale: The sound department must construct an authentic auditory landscape for high-density mainframe spaces and remote faculty offices.
boxes.summary: Server rooms required specialized acoustic planning governed by mid-century standards like ISO 495:1966. Facilities generated steady mechanical sound profiles through cooling blowers and raised-floor airflow systems. Data handling equipment produced continuous hums and localized noise emissions. Mechanical keyboards and equipment operations contributed distinct percussive strikes within testing environments.

boxes.name: CAMPUS ARCHITECTURAL BRUTALISM
boxes.description: Document floor plans, building materials, lighting schemes, and interior finishes of MIT Building 26 and surrounding mid-century Cambridge academic complexes.
boxes.rationale: The production must scout or fabricate accurate institutional spaces featuring exposed concrete, fluorescent lighting tubes, and period linoleum flooring.
boxes.summary: The MIT campus environment centered on mid-century functional complexes including Building 26 and temporary structures like Building 20. The Cambridge facilities utilized concrete, utilitarian interior finishes, and planned institutional lighting layouts. Campus base maps and municipal survey records show connected academic wings organized along Vassar Street and Massachusetts Avenue. Interior corridors connected research laboratories directly to machine suites.

boxes.name: ACADEMIC DRESS CODES
boxes.description: Catalog vintage yearbooks, faculty directories, and personal snapshot collections showing the everyday clothing of computer science researchers, administrative secretaries, and undergraduate students in 1966.
boxes.rationale: Costumers need precise references for rumpled wool suits, short-sleeved shirts, thin knit ties, cat-eye glasses, and early bohemian student wear.
boxes.summary: Archival yearbooks from the MIT Class of 1966 illustrate the everyday attire of students, faculty, and research personnel. Academic staff wore mid-1960s tailored clothing including collared shirts, ties, and sport coats. Administrative staff and female secretaries wore standard period office dresses and skirt sets. Photographic collections from 1966 capture informal campus wear alongside formal institutional portraiture.

boxes.name: VIETNAM WAR PROTESTS
boxes.description: Compile contemporary reports, flyers, and police logs concerning anti-war rallies, draft card resistance, and student radical organizing across Cambridge and Boston during 1966.
boxes.rationale: The script requires accurate political context to reflect campus tensions regarding university military contracts and government-funded computation research.
boxes.summary: Political resistance against the Vietnam War expanded across the Cambridge and Boston areas during 1966. Students for a Democratic Society organized protest marches drawing radical student factions. Activists engaged in public draft card burnings that triggered legal challenges covered by local newspapers. Street demonstrations and anti-war canvassing occurred directly across collegiate grounds.

boxes.name: EARLY HACKER LEXICON
boxes.description: Review period laboratory correspondence, MIT Artificial Intelligence memos, and early computer culture publications for 1966 academic jargon, programmer slang, and administrative shorthand.
boxes.rationale: Dialogue must sound natural to specialized mathematicians and early coders without introducing anachronistic computer terminology.
boxes.summary: Laboratory correspondence and early Artificial Intelligence memos recorded specialized vocabulary emerging from MIT computer culture. Technical teams communicated through structured internal working papers and technical reports. The AI Group established early jargon to describe system processes, routines, and experimental code. These linguistic patterns formed the baseline dialect of Cambridge laboratory personnel.

boxes.name: DEFENSE FUNDING CHANNELS
boxes.description: Research declassified grant summaries, DARPA contracts, and administrative budgets for MIT Project MAC and the Artificial Intelligence Group during the mid-1960s.
boxes.rationale: Writers need to establish the precise bureaucratic pressures and financial relationships driving artificial intelligence research during the Cold War.
boxes.summary: Project MAC received direct funding from the Advanced Research Projects Agency through its Information Processing Techniques Office. Military contracts also originated from the Office of Naval Research. Budget files from Series 5 show that the Artificial Intelligence Group operated under independent funding channels. A full third of early core financial support was directed into targeted laboratory grants.

boxes.name: CAMBRIDGE DAILY LIFE
boxes.description: Survey 1966 street maps, transit records, diner menus, commercial storefronts, and brand packaging from Kendall Square and Central Square.
boxes.rationale: Set dressers and prop masters must accurately dress urban exteriors, cafeteria tables, faculty desks, and neighborhood transit stops.
boxes.summary: Kendall Square and Central Square provided commercial amenities to the MIT community along Massachusetts Avenue. Mid-century retail maps and municipal photographs detail local diners, storefronts, and small service businesses. The surrounding neighborhood underwent active urban renewal projects during the mid-1960s. Cambridge streets accommodated pedestrian transit between campus borders and commercial centers.

boxes.name: CAMPUS SECRECY PROTOCOLS
boxes.description: Examine historical campus police logs, security clearance badges, building access rosters, and visitor procedures for secure research labs at MIT in 1966.
boxes.rationale: Set decorators and background coordinators must visually establish the physical security boundaries separating open classrooms from defense-funded computer installations.
boxes.summary: Campus police maintained official daily logs monitoring building security, personal safety, and visitor access. Secure research facilities operated under specific building access rosters. Campus visitor guidelines managed institutional entries across specialized laboratories. Security divisions coordinated incident reporting and emergency dispatches throughout academic blocks.

boxes.name: PSYCHOANALYTIC PRACTICE PATTERNS
boxes.description: Analyze contemporary clinical literature, popular psychotherapeutic paperback covers, and transcript formats used in Rogerian non-directive counseling during the mid-1960s.
boxes.rationale: The creative team must understand the therapeutic conventions Joseph Weizenbaum consciously modeled when programming the ELIZA script.
boxes.summary: Rogerian therapy applied non-directive counseling methods founded by Carl Rogers. Clinical sessions relied on therapists mirroring patient statements without offering advice or clinical direction. Published session transcripts recorded conversations labeled strictly between counselor and client. Mid-1960s psychotherapeutic paperbacks and literature popularized this reflective conversational format.

boxes.name: SECRETARIAL AND DATA POOL LABOR
boxes.description: Examine archival records, daily logs, oral histories, and photographs documenting the female typists, keypunch operators, and department secretaries whose emotional reactions to ELIZA famously triggered Weizenbaum's ethical concerns.
boxes.rationale: This workforce bridges Computing Hardware Interfaces, Academic Dress Codes, Campus Secrecy Protocols, and Psychoanalytic Practice Patterns as the primary intermediaries interacting with the machine and exemplifying the ELIZA effect.
boxes.summary: Female administrative typists, keypunch workers, and secretaries staffed the daily operations of Project MAC. Joseph Weizenbaum deployed his ELIZA script simulating a Rogerian psychotherapist in this office ecosystem in 1966. The program parsed conversational input and reflected text back to the terminal. Staff members formed rapid personal attachments to the terminal screen, generating the ethical crisis documented in Weizenbaum's retrospective publications.

The original Jargon File was a collection of hacker jargon from technical cultures including the MIT AI Lab, the Stanford AI lab (SAIL), and others of the old ARPANET AI/LISP/PDP-10 communities including Bolt, Beranek and Newman (BBN), Carnegie-Mellon University (CMU), and Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI). The Jargon File (hereafter referred to as ‘jargon-1’ or ‘the File’) was begun by Raphael Finkel at Stanford in 1975. From this time until the plug was finally pulled on the SAIL computer in 1991, the File was named AIWORD.RF[UP,DOC] there. Some terms in it date back considerably earlier ( frob and some senses of moby , for instance, go back to the Tech Model Railroad Club at MIT and are believed to date at least back to the early 1960s)

# Project MAC

Thu, 05/14/1964 - 12:00

One of the first major efforts supported by ARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office (IPTO) was the Project on Mathematics and Computation (Project MAC), the world’s first large-scale experiment in personal computing, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). Orchestrated within the general context of broad-based command and control research suggested by the Office of the Secretary of Defense, and based on the vision of the founding IPTO Director, J.C.R. Licklider, Project MAC was oriented toward achieving a new level of human-computer interaction. A major thrust of Project MAC was to develop general purpose time-sharing capabilities, which later influenced the design of computer systems for commercial and defense uses. Within years of its start, Project MAC would evolve into the world’s first online community, complete with online bulletin boards, email, virtual friendships, an open-source software exchange—and hackers.

The **history of artificial intelligence** began in antiquity, with myths, stories and rumors of artificial beings endowed with intelligence or consciousness by master craftsmen; as Pamela McCorduck writes, AI began with "an ancient wish to forge the gods." [1]

The seeds of modern AI were planted by classical philosophers who attempted to describe the process of human thinking as the mechanical manipulation of symbols. Russell Call Number: BF109 .R6 2002 ISBN: 1883955319 Publication Date: 2002-06-01 This book is the closest thing to an autobiography Rogers left behind. Rogers was a great believer in the value of taping or transcribing client sessions, so it is perhaps unsurprising that this book takes the form of a series of transcribed interviews taped over the course of several months during the next-to-last year of Rogers' life. Perhaps unsurprisingly for a professional therapist, Rogers was a fantastic interview subject--humble, perceptive, and equipped with a capacious memory.
This book goes beyond autobiography in that it is as much concerned with the birth, growth, and development of person-centered therapy as a whole, as it is with the biographical details of Rogers life. The interviews offer Rogers the opportunity to appraise the state of the field of psychotherapy as a whole, as well as his own contributions to it.

**Public entrances**

Much of the MIT campus is open to the general public between the hours of 6 a.m. and 7 p.m. on weekdays, Monday through Friday, except during holidays and Institute closures.

# ELIZA

### A program for simulating understanding and intelligence

Between 1964 and 1966, Joseph Weizenbaum, at the time Associate Professor at MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), developed "ELIZA – A Computer Program For the Study of Natural Language Communication Between Man and Machine". This program consisted of a formal language analyzer that allowed users to converse with it via keyboard. The question-and-answer style of the script simulated a psychotherapist, based on the person-centered therapy of psychotherapist Carl Rogers.

Weizenbaum's original intention with this program was to study the communication between humans and machines, show its superficiality, and demonstrate how easy it is to simulate understanding. To Weizenbaum's dismay, many participants engaged in serious conversations with ELIZA, confiding intimate and emotional details to the machine. Some participants not only developed a close relationship with ELIZA but also attributed empathy to the program. Even some practicing psychotherapists believed that the program could automate talk therapy.
